subject: feminism
title: Wages for Housework: the International Feminist Collective's 1972–1977 campaign demanding pay for domestic labor, the Marxist-feminist debate, and its afterlife in social reproduction theory
dek: How Mariarosa Dalla Costa, Selma James, Silvia Federici, and Brigitte Galtier founded the International Wages for Housework Campaign in Padua in 1972, arguing that unwaged housework is productive labor essential to capitalism; how the campaign spread through New York, London, Toronto, and Italian groups including Black Women for Wages for Housework and Wages Due Lesbians; how Marxist feminists debated whether wages would entrench the gendered division of labor or reveal women's hidden exploitation; and how the analysis resurfaced in social reproduction theory, care-work debates, and calls for basic income from the 2000s onward.
era: International Feminist Collective founded 1972 in Padua; Dalla Costa and James's The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community 1972; Wages for Housework groups active 1972–1977; Federici's Wages Against Housework 1975; domestic labour debate 1970s; Iceland women's day off 24 October 1975; Angela Davis's Women, Race & Class critique 1981; Global Women's Strike from 2000; social reproduction theory 2010s
honesty: This lesson treats Wages for Housework as a specific historical campaign with dated organizations, texts, and debates, not as a settled demand that feminists agreed upon. The core arc follows the 1972 founding in Padua by Mariarosa Dalla Costa, Selma James, Silvia Federici, and Brigitte Galtier; the publication of Dalla Costa and James's The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community (1972); Federici's Wages Against Housework pamphlet (1975); the formation of groups in New York, London (Power of Women Collective), Toronto, and Italy; the emergence of Black Women for Wages for Housework (co-founded by Margaret Prescod and Wilmette Brown) and Wages Due Lesbians; and the domestic labour debate among Marxist feminists who worried that wages would cement rather than challenge the gendered division of labor. Angela Davis's Women, Race & Class (1981) critiqued the campaign for potentially reinforcing women's confinement to the home. The Elsewhere section covers the Icelandic women's day off on 24 October 1975, when approximately 90% of Icelandic women stopped paid and unpaid work, and the UN International Women's Year 1975 conference in Mexico City—contemporaneous global actions on women's labor. The After section traces how the analysis resurfaced in Federici's Caliban and the Witch (2004), in social reproduction theory debates from the 2010s, in care-work scholarship, and in basic income proposals. Related links point to second-wave feminism, care ethics, standpoint theory, and intersectionality lessons already in the capsules collection.

timeline.label: Marx and Engels: The Communist Manifesto
timeline.detail: Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels publish The Communist Manifesto, analyzing capitalism and class struggle. Later Marxist feminists will debate how Marx's concept of productive labor excludes unwaged domestic work—a gap the Wages for Housework campaign addresses.

timeline.label: Marx: Capital Vol. 1 and the reproduction of labor-power
timeline.detail: Marx's Capital analyzes how workers sell labor-power and how capital requires the daily and generational reproduction of that labor-power. But Marx treats reproduction as outside the process of surplus-value extraction, laying groundwork for Wages for Housework theorists to critique his framework.

timeline.label: Betty Friedan: The Feminine Mystique
timeline.detail: Friedan's The Feminine Mystique describes the malaise of middle-class American housewives confined to domesticity. While Friedan advocates entry into paid work as liberation, Wages for Housework will later argue that this doubles women's labor without challenging capitalism's reliance on unpaid housework.

timeline.label: Margaret Benston: 'The Political Economy of Women's Liberation'
timeline.detail: Benston publishes an early essay arguing that women's work in the home constitutes a separate mode of production. This sparks the domestic labour debate among Marxist feminists in the early 1970s.

timeline.label: International Feminist Collective founded in Padua
timeline.detail: In Padua, Italy, Mariarosa Dalla Costa, Selma James, Silvia Federici, and Brigitte Galtier co-found the International Feminist Collective and issue the founding statement launching the Wages for Housework campaign.

timeline.label: Dalla Costa and James: The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community
timeline.detail: Mariarosa Dalla Costa and Selma James publish The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community (Falling Wall Press, Bristol). The pamphlet argues that housework is productive labor that produces and reproduces labor-power, making it central to capitalist accumulation.

timeline.label: New York committee's first flyer
timeline.detail: The New York Wages for Housework Committee, which Silvia Federici helped found, distributes its first flyer, 'We Can't Afford to Work for Love.' In 1975 it opens a storefront office in Brooklyn.

timeline.label: Power of Women Collective in London and Bristol
timeline.detail: After the 1972 National Women's Liberation Conference in Manchester, Selma James and a few other women form the Power of Women Collective in London and Bristol. It publishes a journal, Power of Women, and in 1975 it is reconstituted as the Wages for Housework Campaign.

timeline.label: Toronto Wages for Housework Committee
timeline.detail: The Toronto Wages for Housework Committee is founded and becomes one of the most active groups in the campaign in Canada.

timeline.label: Silvia Federici: Wages Against Housework
timeline.detail: Federici publishes the pamphlet Wages Against Housework (Power of Women Collective and Falling Wall Press). Despite the title, it argues for the demand as a strategy to make women's invisible labor visible and to refuse the naturalization of housework as love rather than work.

timeline.label: Black Women for Wages for Housework
timeline.detail: Margaret Prescod and Wilmette Brown co-found Black Women for Wages for Housework in New York to center race in the campaign, pointing out that Black women and other women of color often do paid domestic work in other people's homes as well as unpaid work in their own.

timeline.label: Iceland women's day off: 24 October 1975
timeline.detail: Approximately 90% of Icelandic women stop paid work and refuse housework and childcare for one day, demonstrating the indispensability of women's labor. The day becomes known as Kvennafrídagurinn (Women's Day Off). Iceland passes an equal-rights law the following year.

timeline.label: UN International Women's Year and Mexico City conference
timeline.detail: The United Nations declares 1975 International Women's Year and convenes the first World Conference on Women in Mexico City (June–July 1975). Delegates debate women's labor, development, and equality—though Wages for Housework remains a minority radical position.

timeline.label: Wages Due Lesbians
timeline.detail: Lesbian members of the Toronto Wages for Housework Committee form Wages Due Lesbians, arguing that women's economic dependence on men enforces heterosexuality and that the wage demand is therefore a lesbian issue. Francie Wyland writes on custody, motherhood and lesbianism.

timeline.label: The domestic labour debate
timeline.detail: Marxist feminist theorists including Wally Seccombe, Jean Gardiner, and others debate whether housework produces value, whether it is productive or unproductive labor in Marx's sense, and whether the demand for wages is strategically useful or a trap that naturalizes women's domestic role.

timeline.label: Angela Davis: Women, Race & Class critique
timeline.detail: Davis publishes Women, Race & Class. Its final chapter argues that Black women's long experience of paid domestic service shows a wage does not make housework less isolating or degrading, and calls for socializing housework instead.

timeline.label: Global Women's Strike launched
timeline.detail: On 8 March 2000, the Global Women's Strike is launched in dozens of countries, calling for recognition and payment of women's unwaged caring work. Selma James is a key organizer. The strike revives Wages for Housework arguments in the context of neoliberal globalization.

timeline.label: Silvia Federici: Caliban and the Witch
timeline.detail: Federici publishes Caliban and the Witch: Women, the Body and Primitive Accumulation (Autonomedia). The book reinterprets the European witch-hunts and enclosures as strategies to control women's bodies and reproduction, extending the Wages for Housework analysis into a historical account of capitalism's origins.

timeline.label: Social reproduction theory and care-work debates
timeline.detail: A new generation of Marxist feminists—including Tithi Bhattacharya, Cinzia Arruzza, and Nancy Fraser—revive and refine social reproduction theory, analyzing how capitalism depends on the unwaged or underpaid labor of caring, cleaning, feeding, and raising the next generation.

timeline.label: Silvia Federici: Revolution at Point Zero
timeline.detail: Federici publishes Revolution at Point Zero: Housework, Reproduction, and Feminist Struggle (PM Press), collecting essays spanning four decades. The book reintroduces Wages for Housework texts to a new feminist audience amid austerity, precarity, and care crises.

read.title: Mariarosa Dalla Costa and Selma James — The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community (Falling Wall Press, 1972)
read.note: The founding pamphlet. Dalla Costa's essay argues that housework produces labor-power, the commodity workers sell, and James's writing places the demand in the context of unwaged work around the world. Full text on libcom.org.

read.title: Silvia Federici — Wages Against Housework (1975)
read.note: Federici's clearest statement. Despite the title, it argues for the wage demand as a political strategy to denaturalize housework, make invisible labor visible, and refuse the ideology that women do housework out of love rather than economic necessity. Open-access PDF.

read.title: Silvia Federici — Caliban and the Witch: Women, the Body and Primitive Accumulation (Autonomedia, 2004)
read.note: Federici's major book extending the Wages for Housework analysis historically. Argues that the European witch-hunts, enclosures, and colonization were strategies to discipline women's bodies, control reproduction, and establish the unpaid domestic sphere that capitalism requires. Widely taught. Wikipedia entry.

read.title: Silvia Federici — Revolution at Point Zero: Housework, Reproduction, and Feminist Struggle (PM Press, 2012; expanded second edition 2020)
read.note: Federici's essays from the Wages for Housework years onward, on housework, the globalization of care work, elder care and the commons. The 2020 second edition adds three essays. Publisher page.

read.title: Angela Davis — Women, Race & Class (Random House, 1981)
read.note: Davis's classic includes a chapter critiquing middle-class feminist campaigns that ignore how Black women's labor history—slavery, sharecropping, domestic service for whites—makes 'return to the home' an inadequate frame. Essential counterpoint. Wikipedia entry.

read.title: Tithi Bhattacharya, ed. — Social Reproduction Theory: Remapping Class, Recentering Oppression (Pluto Press, 2017)
read.note: Contemporary collection reviving and refining the Wages for Housework analysis through social reproduction theory. Essays by Bhattacharya, Cinzia Arruzza, Susan Ferguson, and others analyze how capitalism depends on unwaged care work. Publisher page.

read.title: Leopoldina Fortunati — The Arcane of Reproduction: Housework, Prostitution, Labor and Capital (Autonomedia, 1995; original Italian 1981)
read.note: Fortunati, an Italian autonomist feminist, extends the Wages for Housework argument, analyzing prostitution alongside housework. Full text hosted on libcom.org.

read.title: Wikipedia — Wages for Housework
read.note: Open encyclopedia entry covering the campaign's history, key figures, arguments, criticisms, and legacy. Includes timeline and bibliography.

read.title: Wikipedia — 1975 Icelandic Women's Strike
read.note: Open entry on the 24 October 1975 women's day off in Iceland, when 90% of women stopped paid and unpaid work. Contextualizes Wages for Housework within contemporaneous direct action.

read.title: Wikipedia — Selma James
read.note: Biography of Selma James (born 1930), American-British feminist, co-founder of the International Feminist Collective and the Power of Women Collective, and long-time organizer with the Global Women's Strike.

read.title: Wikipedia — Silvia Federici
read.note: Biography of Silvia Federici (born 1942), Italian-American scholar and activist, co-founder of the New York Wages for Housework Committee, author of Caliban and the Witch and Revolution at Point Zero.

read.title: Wikipedia — Mariarosa Dalla Costa
read.note: Biography of Mariarosa Dalla Costa (born 1943), Italian autonomist feminist, co-author of The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community, member of Lotta Femminista, and co-founder of the International Feminist Collective.

fun_fact.title: Wages Against Housework argued for wages, not against them
fun_fact.text: Silvia Federici's 1975 pamphlet title Wages Against Housework confuses readers to this day. The title does not mean 'against paying for housework'; it means wages as a weapon against the institution of housework. Federici explains that demanding wages is a political strategy to denaturalize the idea that women do housework out of love, maternal instinct, or feminine nature rather than economic coercion. The wage demand makes visible the fact that housework is work—socially necessary labor that capital relies on but refuses to pay for. Once recognized as work, housework can be refused, organized against, or shared rather than romanticized as women's destiny. The title's ambiguity captures the paradox: the campaign demanded wages not because wages would liberate women, but because the demand itself would expose how capitalism depends on a vast reservoir of unpaid female labor.

glossary.explain: A feminist campaign launched in 1972 demanding that women be paid by the state for the work of cooking, cleaning, childcare, and other domestic labor—work that the campaign argued is essential to capitalist production but made invisible and unpaid.

The network founded at a 1972 meeting in Padua, Italy, by a group that included Mariarosa Dalla Costa, Selma James, Silvia Federici and Brigitte Galtier, which launched the Wages for Housework demand internationally.

Italian autonomist feminist (born 1943), member of Lotta Femminista, co-author with Selma James of The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community (1972), and co-founder of the International Feminist Collective.

American-British feminist activist and writer (born 1930), co-author of The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community (1972), co-founder of the International Feminist Collective and the Power of Women Collective in London, and organizer of the Global Women's Strike from 2000.

Italian-American feminist scholar and activist (born 1942), co-founder of the International Feminist Collective and the New York Wages for Housework Committee, author of Wages Against Housework (1975), Caliban and the Witch (2004), and Revolution at Point Zero (2012).
French feminist, one of the founders of the International Feminist Collective in Padua in 1972, alongside Dalla Costa, James and Federici.

glossary.term: The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community
aliases: Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community
glossary.explain: The 1972 pamphlet by Mariarosa Dalla Costa (essay) and Selma James (preface), published by Falling Wall Press in Bristol. The founding text of the Wages for Housework campaign, arguing that housework is productive labor that produces and reproduces labor-power.

Silvia Federici's 1975 pamphlet published by Power of Women Collective and Falling Wall Press. Despite the ambiguous title, it argues for the wage demand as a strategy to make invisible labor visible and to denaturalize the ideology that women do housework for love.

The work of bearing, raising, feeding, clothing, cleaning, and caring for workers—reproducing labor-power on a daily and generational basis. Wages for Housework theorists argue this labor is essential to capitalism but unwaged and naturalized as women's duty.

In Marxist theory, labor that produces surplus value for capital. Classical Marxism treated only wage labor in commodity production as productive. Wages for Housework theorists argued that housework is productive because it produces labor-power, the commodity workers sell.

The capacity to work that workers sell to capitalists for a wage. Marx analyzed how capital buys labor-power and extracts surplus value. Wages for Housework theorists argued that housework produces and reproduces this capacity, making it productive labor capital refuses to pay for.

The 1970s Marxist feminist debate over whether housework produces value, whether it is productive or unproductive labor in Marx's technical sense, and whether the demand for wages is politically useful or a trap. Key contributors included Wally Seccombe, Jean Gardiner, and Heidi Hartmann.

Work done without a wage. Wages for Housework emphasized that housework is work—socially necessary labor—but capital's refusal to pay for it keeps it invisible and naturalized as love, duty, or women's nature.

glossary.term: New York Wages for Housework Committee
glossary.explain: The New York group that Silvia Federici and others formed in the early 1970s. Its first flyer appeared in 1973, and in 1975 it opened a storefront office in Brooklyn. It dissolved in 1977.

The London-based Wages for Housework group organized by Selma James and others. Published the journal Power of Women (printed by Falling Wall Press in Bristol) from 1974, collecting international feminist writings on unwaged labor.
The Canadian Wages for Housework group founded in Toronto in 1975, one of the most active in the campaign. Wages Due Lesbians grew out of it.

glossary.term: Black Women for Wages for Housework
glossary.explain: A group within the Wages for Housework campaign, led by Wilmette Brown and others, that centered race in the analysis. Pointed out that Black women disproportionately perform both paid domestic work in white households and unpaid work in their own, making the wage demand urgent for combating racial and gender exploitation simultaneously.

American activist who co-founded Black Women for Wages for Housework in New York with Margaret Prescod and later worked from London. Wrote and organized to connect the wage demand with anti-racism, pointing out that women of color subsidize capital and white households through underpaid and unpaid labor.

A group formed by lesbian members of the Toronto Wages for Housework Committee in the mid-1970s. It argued that women's economic dependence on men enforces heterosexuality, so lesbians pay an economic penalty, which makes wages for housework a lesbian issue. It continues today as Queer Strike.
Toronto member of Wages for Housework and Wages Due Lesbians who wrote on lesbian motherhood, child custody and the case for wages for housework.

The work of cooking, cleaning, shopping, laundry, childcare, and other tasks required to maintain a household and reproduce labor-power. Wages for Housework argued this is work essential to capitalism but made invisible by being unwaged and naturalized as women's love or duty.

Italian feminist movement (the name means Feminist Struggle). Mariarosa Dalla Costa was a member. Lotta Femminista developed autonomist feminist analysis linking housework to capitalist exploitation and women's position to broader class struggle.

A strand of Marxist theory emerging in Italy in the 1960s–1970s emphasizing workers' autonomy and refusal of work as the motor of capitalist crisis. Wages for Housework theorists extended this analysis to unwaged domestic labor and women's refusal.

American political activist, scholar, and author (born 1944). In Women, Race & Class (1981), Davis critiques middle-class feminist demands like Wages for Housework for ignoring how Black women's history includes coerced labor in white households and their own, making domesticity a white bourgeois frame.

Angela Davis's 1981 book (Random House) analyzing intersections of racism, sexism, and class in U.S. history. Includes a critique of campaigns like Wages for Housework for potentially reinforcing women's confinement to domestic roles.

On 24 October 1975, approximately 90% of Icelandic women stopped paid work and refused housework and childcare for one day, demonstrating the indispensability of women's labor. Iceland passed an equal-rights law the following year.

The United Nations declared 1975 International Women's Year and convened the first World Conference on Women in Mexico City (June–July 1975). Delegates debated women's labor, development, and equality, though Wages for Housework remained a minority radical position.

A campaign launched on 8 March 2000 in dozens of countries calling for recognition and payment of women's unwaged work—caring, cleaning, cooking, raising children. Selma James was a key organizer. Revived Wages for Housework arguments in the context of neoliberal globalization.

aliases: Caliban and the Witch: Women, the Body and Primitive Accumulation
glossary.explain: Silvia Federici's 2004 book (Autonomedia). Reinterprets the European witch-hunts, enclosures, and colonization as strategies to control women's bodies and reproduction, establishing the unpaid domestic sphere capitalism requires. Extends the Wages for Housework analysis historically.

A strand of Marxist feminist theory arguing that capitalism depends on the reproduction of labor-power—the daily and generational work of caring, feeding, cleaning, raising children—most of which is unwaged or underpaid. Revives and refines the Wages for Housework analysis in the 2010s. Key theorists include Tithi Bhattacharya, Cinzia Arruzza, Nancy Fraser.

In Marx's Capital, the historical process by which peasants were separated from land and turned into wage laborers—the violent origin of capitalism. Federici reinterprets witch-hunts and the creation of the unwaged domestic sphere as forms of primitive accumulation targeting women's bodies and labor.

The historical process of privatizing common land in Europe, forcing peasants off the land and into wage labor. Federici links enclosures to the disciplining of women and the creation of the domestic sphere as an unpaid zone of reproduction.

The labor of caring for dependents—children, elderly, sick, disabled. Contemporary feminist political economy debates how care work is distributed, who pays for it, and how its undervaluation structures gender, race, and class hierarchies. Wages for Housework prefigured these debates.

A policy proposal to give all citizens a regular, unconditional cash payment. Some feminists link basic income to the Wages for Housework demand, arguing it would recognize unwaged reproductive labor; others worry it could subsidize capital by keeping wages low.

Indian-American Marxist feminist scholar and organizer. Editor of Social Reproduction Theory (2017), which collects essays reviving the Wages for Housework analysis in the context of contemporary capitalism, austerity, and feminist strikes.

Italian philosopher and feminist activist. Co-author of Feminism for the 99% (2019) and contributor to contemporary social reproduction theory debates, analyzing how capitalism depends on unwaged care and domestic labor.

American philosopher and critical theorist (born 1947). In works like Fortunes of Feminism (2013) and Cannibal Capitalism (2022), Fraser analyzes how capitalism relies on and cannibalizes the unwaged work of social reproduction—care, education, community.

Italian feminist theorist. Author of The Arcane of Reproduction (1981, English 1995), which extends the Wages for Housework argument by analyzing housework and prostitution as two forms of reproductive labor essential to but hidden by capitalism.

aliases: Revolution at Point Zero: Housework, Reproduction, and Feminist Struggle
glossary.explain: Silvia Federici's 2012 essay collection (PM Press) spanning four decades. Reprints Wages for Housework texts and later essays on globalization, reproductive labor, and care crises, introducing the analysis to a new generation.

A Bristol-based radical press that published early Wages for Housework pamphlets, including Dalla Costa and James's The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community (1972) and Federici's Wages Against Housework (1975).

American feminist writer and activist (1921–2006). Author of The Feminine Mystique (1963), which critiqued the confinement of middle-class women to domesticity and urged entry into paid work. Wages for Housework theorists later argued this doubled women's labor without challenging capitalism's reliance on unpaid housework.

Betty Friedan's 1963 book describing the malaise of middle-class American housewives confined to suburban domesticity. Friedan advocated careers and paid work as liberation; Wages for Housework critiqued this as ignoring that capital requires unpaid domestic labor whether women also work outside the home or not.

The resurgence of feminist activism and theory from the 1960s through the 1980s in the U.S. and Europe. Wages for Housework emerged within the radical wing of second-wave feminism, critiquing liberal feminism's focus on workplace equality while capital continued to rely on unpaid housework.

A second-wave feminist slogan asserting that experiences labeled private—housework, sexuality, childcare, domestic violence—are structured by political power relations. Wages for Housework applied this to argue that the unwaged status of housework is a political decision, not a natural fact.

Canadian chemist and feminist. Her 1969 essay 'The Political Economy of Women's Liberation' argued that women's work in the home constitutes a separate mode of production, sparking the domestic labour debate among Marxist feminists.

Canadian Marxist who participated in the domestic labour debate, arguing about whether housework produces value. His positions were debated and critiqued by Wages for Housework theorists and other Marxist feminists.
British economist and feminist who contributed to the domestic labour debate in the 1970s, analyzing women's economic dependency and the relationship between housework and wage labor.

American feminist economist. Author of 'The Unhappy Marriage of Marxism and Feminism' (1979), arguing that Marxist analysis alone cannot explain women's oppression and that patriarchy and capitalism must be analyzed as dual systems.
Barbados-born activist who co-founded Black Women for Wages for Housework in New York with Wilmette Brown in 1975.

sections.title: Before Wages for Housework: Marx treating housework as outside production, Friedan-era framing, and second-wave consciousness-raising

blocks.text: Karl Marx's Capital (1867) analyzed how capitalists buy labor-power—the capacity to work—and extract surplus value from its use. Marx noted that labor-power must be reproduced daily (workers need food, rest, shelter) and generationally (new workers must be born and raised). But he treated this reproduction as outside the sphere of capitalist production proper. Women's work in the home—cooking, cleaning, childcare—appeared in Marx's account as part of the worker's consumption, not as labor that produces value. This framing set the terms for a century of Marxist theory that ignored or naturalized housework as a precondition for wage labor rather than as labor itself.

Mid-twentieth-century liberal feminism, exemplified by Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963), critiqued the confinement of middle-class American women to suburban domesticity and urged women to seek careers and fulfillment in paid work. Friedan's diagnosis was psychological and individualist: housework was deadening, and liberation meant entering the public world of employment. What this framing missed—and what the Wages for Housework campaign would later emphasize—was that capital benefits whether women do only unpaid housework or whether they do both paid work outside the home and unpaid work inside it. Either way, someone has to cook, clean, and raise children, and capital refuses to pay for most of that labor.

By the late 1960s, second-wave feminism's radical wing was practicing consciousness-raising: small groups of women sharing personal experiences to identify systemic patterns. The slogan 'the personal is political' named the insight that what seemed like private troubles—housework drudgery, economic dependence on men, exhaustion—were structured by political and economic relations. This grassroots practice prepared the ground for the theoretical leap the Wages for Housework campaign would make: that housework is not a personal service women perform out of love but a form of labor that capital extracts without paying.

sections.title: What Wages for Housework claimed: housework as productive labor that reproduces labor-power, unwaged and thus invisible, essential to capitalist accumulation

blocks.text: The Wages for Housework argument rested on a reinterpretation of Marxist value theory. In classical Marxism, productive labor is labor that produces surplus value for capital—labor performed under capitalist relations of production for a wage. Housework seemed to fall outside: it is unwaged, done in the private home, and its products—meals, clean clothes, cared-for children—are consumed by the family, not sold as commodities. But Wages for Housework theorists argued that this is a mystification. Housework does produce a commodity: labor-power itself. Workers sell their capacity to work to capitalists. That capacity must be produced and reproduced daily—workers need to be fed, clothed, rested—and generationally—children must be born, raised, trained. All of this work is done disproportionately by women, unwaged, in the home.

If housework produces labor-power, then it is productive labor essential to capitalist accumulation. Capital pays workers a wage supposedly sufficient to reproduce labor-power, but in fact that wage covers only the commodities purchased—food, rent, utilities. The labor of transforming those commodities into usable form—cooking the food, cleaning the house, caring for children—is unpaid. It is unwaged labor that capital appropriates. The wage relation thus hides a vast reservoir of exploitation: women's unpaid work subsidizes capital by keeping the wage bill low. Capital does not have to pay for the full cost of reproducing the working class because it externalizes that cost onto women in the home.

The demand for wages was a political strategy, not an economic reform proposal. Wages for Housework organizers did not expect capitalists or the state to start paying women salaries for cooking and cleaning. The demand was intended to make visible what had been naturalized as invisible. Calling housework 'work' and demanding a wage for it denaturalized the ideology that women do domestic labor out of love, maternal instinct, or feminine nature. It named housework as labor and named the wage relation's refusal to pay for it as exploitation. The demand also implied the possibility of refusal: if housework is work, women can refuse to do it, strike against it, or demand that it be socialized and shared rather than privatized and assigned to women.

sections.title: Padua 1972: Dalla Costa, James, Federici, Galtier, and the founding of the International Feminist Collective

blocks.text: In 1972, at a meeting in Padua, Italy, a small group of women that included Mariarosa Dalla Costa, Selma James, Silvia Federici and Brigitte Galtier founded the International Feminist Collective, which launched the Wages for Housework campaign. Mariarosa Dalla Costa was a member of Lotta Femminista (Feminist Struggle), an Italian autonomist feminist movement emerging from the New Left and operaismo—Italian workerism. Selma James was an American-born activist living in Britain who had organized with C. L. R. James and later developed feminist analysis linking women's unwaged labor to broader struggles. Silvia Federici had moved from Italy to the United States to study philosophy; she was becoming active in feminist organizing. Brigitte Galtier was a French feminist. Together they drafted the statement founding the International Feminist Collective and articulated the demand that housework be recognized and paid as work.

Also in 1972, Falling Wall Press in Bristol published The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community, a pamphlet with an essay by Dalla Costa and a preface by James. This became the founding text. Dalla Costa's essay argued that housework is not peripheral to capitalism but central. Women's labor in the home produces and reproduces labor-power, the commodity that capital buys when it hires workers. Because this labor is unwaged, it is invisible: it appears as a natural service women provide rather than as work capital exploits. Dalla Costa argued that recognizing housework as productive labor changes the political terrain. Women are not merely oppressed by men in the private sphere; they are exploited by capital through the wage relation's refusal to pay for reproductive labor. This analysis linked women's domestic struggle to class struggle and opened the possibility of women refusing housework as a form of strike against capital.

blocks.alt: Selma James, an older woman with short white hair and a tweed jacket, speaking.
blocks.caption: Selma James speaking at a workshop at the Left Forum in New York on 17 March 2012. She co-wrote The Power of Women and the Subversion of the Community in 1972 and was still organizing with the Global Women's Strike forty years later.

blocks.text: James's preface situated the argument globally. She pointed out that most of the world's women do unwaged work—not only housework in Western nuclear families but subsistence farming, informal sector labor, community care. Wages for Housework was not a demand for middle-class housewives alone; it was a way of naming how capital structures a global division between waged and unwaged labor, with women, colonized peoples, and racialized workers disproportionately forced into the unwaged zones that capital depends on but refuses to recognize.

sections.title: New York, London, Toronto, Italy: Wages for Housework committees and the Power of Women Collective, Black Women for Wages for Housework, Wages Due Lesbians

blocks.text: After the 1972 founding, Wages for Housework groups formed in multiple countries. In New York, Silvia Federici and others formed the New York Wages for Housework Committee in the early 1970s. Its first flyer, 'We Can't Afford to Work for Love,' went out in 1973, and in 1975 the committee opened a storefront office in Brooklyn. Around 1974 the Brooklyn group produced a poster that read: 'The Women of the World Are Serving Notice! We want wages for every dirty toilet, every indecent assault, every painful childbirth, every cup of coffee and every smile. And if we don't get what we want we will simply refuse to work any longer!' In London, the Power of Women Collective, organized by Selma James and others, published the journal Power of Women beginning in 1974. The journal was printed by Falling Wall Press in Bristol and collected statements, essays, and documents from Wages for Housework groups internationally.

blocks.alt: Red poster with line drawings of women doing housework and the words No to welfare cuts, Yes to wages for housework from the government for all women.
blocks.caption: Poster for the Wages for Housework and Welfare Conference held on Saturday 24 April 1976, organized by the New York Wages for Housework Committee from its storefront office at 288B Eighth Street in Brooklyn. The committee linked the wage demand to the defence of welfare payments against cuts.

blocks.text: Toronto's Wages for Housework Committee, founded in 1975, became one of the most active groups in Canada, and lesbian members there formed Wages Due Lesbians. This group argued that state-mandated heterosexuality operates through women's economic dependence on men. Because marriage and domestic partnership assign women unpaid housework in exchange for male wages or protection, refusing that arrangement—living as a lesbian outside the heterosexual family—means facing economic punishment. Francie Wyland, a Toronto member, wrote on child custody, motherhood and lesbianism to make the argument: lesbians need economic independence, and the wage demand exposes how compulsory heterosexuality is an economic institution.

In 1975, Black Women for Wages for Housework formed in New York, co-founded by Margaret Prescod and Wilmette Brown. This group insisted that race could not be an afterthought. Black women and women of color in the U.S., Britain, and globally perform both paid domestic labor in white households (as maids, nannies, cleaners) and unpaid labor in their own. They subsidize white middle-class women's entry into professional work and subsidize capital by keeping the cost of social reproduction low. Black Women for Wages for Housework argued that the wage demand was urgent for challenging both racial and gender exploitation: paying for all reproductive labor would force capital and the state to recognize and value work that is currently invisibilized and racialized.

These groups were loose, overlapping, and short-lived as formal organizations. By the late 1970s, most had dissolved or transformed into other projects. But the texts they produced circulated widely, and the debates they sparked—about the relationship between waged and unwaged labor, about whether the home is a site of production, about whether demanding wages traps women in domestic roles or exposes capital's reliance on their unpaid work—continued among Marxist feminists for decades.

sections.title: Federici's Wages Against Housework (1975): why the demand makes invisible labor visible

blocks.text: In 1975, Silvia Federici published Wages Against Housework, a short pamphlet published by the Power of Women Collective and Falling Wall Press. The title is deliberately ambiguous and has confused readers ever since. Federici is not arguing against paying women for housework; she is arguing for wages as a weapon against the institution of housework as unpaid, naturalized, women's destiny. The pamphlet is the clearest short statement of the campaign's strategy.

blocks.alt: Silvia Federici, a woman with short grey hair and a patterned scarf, speaking into a studio microphone.
blocks.caption: Silvia Federici giving a talk at the MACBA museum in Barcelona in May 2012, the year PM Press collected her essays as Revolution at Point Zero.

blocks.text: Federici begins by noting that when housework is called 'work,' the response is often that housework is not real work—it's what women do because they love their families. This ideology is the problem the wage demand targets. Calling housework work and demanding wages for it makes visible the economic coercion behind the appearance of love. Women do housework not because of maternal instinct but because they have no other means of survival. The unwaged status of housework is not a benign oversight; it is a political decision that benefits capital. If housework were waged, the cost of reproducing the working class would be visible on the ledger, and capital would have to pay for it or socialize it.

Federici emphasizes that the demand is not a reformist plea for inclusion in the wage system. Wages for Housework organizers do not want to make housework a respectable career. The demand is a refusal: it refuses the naturalization of women's unpaid labor, it refuses the ideology that links femininity to selfless service, and it refuses to let capital hide the extent of its exploitation. Once housework is recognized as work, it can be collectively refused, and the question becomes: Why should this labor be done by individual women in isolated homes? Why not socialize childcare, communal kitchens, shared laundry? The wage demand opens space for imagining refusal and reorganization.

sections.title: Marxist feminists dispute the strategy: does demanding wages entrench the gendered division of labor or expose capital's dependence on unwaged work?

blocks.text: The Wages for Housework campaign provoked fierce debate among Marxist feminists throughout the 1970s, a conversation known as the domestic labour debate. Some participants, including Wally Seccombe and Jean Gardiner, focused on the theoretical question of whether housework produces value in Marx's sense. If value is socially necessary labor time embodied in commodities, does housework—which produces use-values consumed in the home rather than exchange-values sold on the market—produce value? The debate became intricate and scholastic, but it mattered politically: if housework is unproductive in Marx's technical sense, then the wage demand makes no sense within Marxist categories.

Others worried that demanding wages would entrench rather than challenge the gendered division of labor. If the state paid women to do housework, would that cement the idea that housework is women's work, making it harder to demand that men share it or that it be socialized? Would wages make the home a site of even more intense exploitation rather than a space women could refuse? Heidi Hartmann's influential essay 'The Unhappy Marriage of Marxism and Feminism' (1979) argued that Marxist analysis alone could not explain why housework is assigned to women; patriarchy as a separate system also structures the division of labor. Some feminists saw the wage demand as accommodating patriarchal capitalism rather than challenging it.

Angela Davis's Women, Race & Class (1981) took on the campaign directly in its final chapter, 'The Approaching Obsolescence of Housework: A Working-Class Perspective.' Davis pointed out that Black women in the United States had been paid for housework for generations, as maids, cooks and nannies in white households, and that the wage had not freed them: domestic service remained one of the worst-paid and most degrading kinds of work. She doubted that a government wage would change the isolated, repetitive character of housework, and she worried it would tie women more firmly to the home. Instead she argued for socializing the work through publicly funded childcare, community cooking and cleaning services, and technology that could make most private housework obsolete.

Wages for Housework theorists replied that they were not advocating domesticity. The demand was a strategy for exposing and refusing exploitation, not a plan to keep women in the kitchen. Federici and James emphasized that once housework is recognized as work, it can be refused, organized against, and reimagined. The debate never resolved, but it clarified the stakes: any feminist challenge to capitalism must grapple with the fact that capital depends on a vast reservoir of unwaged labor, disproportionately done by women and racialized workers, and any strategy for liberation must decide whether to demand recognition and payment for that labor or to refuse and abolish it.

sections.title: Same years, parallel actions: Iceland's women's day off on 24 October 1975 and the UN International Women's Year conference in Mexico City

blocks.text: On 24 October 1975, approximately 90% of Icelandic women stopped work. They did not go to their paid jobs, and they did not do housework or childcare. The action was called Kvennafrídagurinn—Women's Day Off—and it was organized by women's organizations to demonstrate the indispensability of women's labor, both waged and unwaged. Schools, shops and fish factories closed, and many fathers had to bring their children to work. About 25,000 people, in a country of about 220,000, gathered for a rally in central Reykjavík. The strike made visible what Wages for Housework had been arguing theoretically: that women's labor—paid and unpaid—is essential to the functioning of society and economy, and that its unwaged status makes it invisible until women refuse to do it. In 1976, Iceland passed legislation guaranteeing equal rights for women and men.

Earlier that year, in June and July 1975, the United Nations convened the first World Conference on Women in Mexico City as part of International Women's Year 1975. Delegations from 133 countries attended, debating development, equality and peace. The conference produced a World Plan of Action calling for legal equality, education, employment, and political participation for women. Wages for Housework was a marginal position at the conference—mainstream delegates focused on integrating women into development and formal employment rather than questioning the wage relation or demanding payment for reproductive labor. But the conference's focus on women's labor, combined with grassroots actions like the Iceland strike, reflected a global moment when feminists worldwide were making women's work—especially unwaged work—politically visible.

sections.title: After the 1970s: the Global Women's Strike from 2000, social reproduction theory in the 2010s, care-work debates, and basic income proposals

blocks.text: By the late 1970s, the Wages for Housework campaign as an organized movement had largely dissolved, though its arguments continued to circulate. In the 1980s and 1990s, neoliberal globalization restructured labor and welfare systems worldwide. Women entered formal employment in unprecedented numbers, but this did not end their responsibility for housework and care. Instead, it created what feminists called the 'double shift' or 'second shift': women working full-time for wages and then doing a full workday of unpaid labor at home. Globally, wealthy households hired domestic workers—disproportionately immigrant women and women of color—to do cleaning, cooking, and childcare at low wages, creating what scholars called 'global care chains': women from the Global South migrating to care for children in the Global North while leaving their own children with relatives or paid caregivers.

On 8 March 2000, the Global Women's Strike was launched in dozens of countries, calling for recognition and payment of women's unwaged work. Selma James was a key organizer. The strike revived the Wages for Housework demand in the context of neoliberal austerity, welfare cuts, and the privatization of social services. The strike connected unwaged care work in the home with underpaid care work in hospitals, schools, and elder care facilities, arguing that capital and the state depend on women's cheap or free labor to reproduce society while cutting public spending.

In 2004, Silvia Federici published Caliban and the Witch: Women, the Body and Primitive Accumulation. The book became a widely taught feminist classic. Federici reinterpreted the European witch-hunts of the early modern period as a campaign to control women's bodies and reproduction at the moment when capitalism was emerging. She argued that enclosures—the privatization of common land—were accompanied by the privatization of reproduction: women were confined to the home and assigned unpaid responsibility for raising the next generation of workers. The witch-hunts targeted women healers, midwives, and women who resisted this new sexual division of labor. Caliban extended the Wages for Housework analysis historically, arguing that capitalism's origins required disciplining women into unwaged domestic labor.

In the 2010s, a new generation of Marxist feminists revived the analysis under the label social reproduction theory. Tithi Bhattacharya edited Social Reproduction Theory: Remapping Class, Recentering Oppression (2017), collecting essays by Bhattacharya, Cinzia Arruzza, Susan Ferguson, and others. Nancy Fraser analyzed how capitalism depends on and cannibalizes the work of social reproduction—care, education, community—in books like Fortunes of Feminism (2013) and Cannibal Capitalism (2022). These theorists argued that capitalism's current crisis includes a crisis of care: austerity cuts social services, wages stagnate, and families cannot afford to pay for childcare or elder care, yet the work must still be done. Social reproduction theory brought Wages for Housework arguments into debates about how to challenge neoliberalism and imagine post-capitalist futures.

The question of how to recognize and redistribute care work remains unresolved. Some feminists advocate universal basic income as a contemporary analogue to Wages for Housework: an unconditional payment that would recognize all labor, waged and unwaged. Others worry that basic income without public services would leave care work privatized and still disproportionately done by women. Care-work scholarship analyzes how care is commodified, outsourced, and racialized in global labor markets. The pandemic of 2020–2021 made the crisis visible: schools and daycares closed, hospitals were overwhelmed, and millions of women left paid employment to do unpaid care work at home. The old Wages for Housework slogan returned: who will pay for the work that keeps society alive?

When you eat a meal someone else cooked, wear clothes someone else washed, or benefit from someone else's care for a child or an elder, do you ask who did that work, whether they were paid, and whose labor subsidizes the economy's claim to efficiency by being naturalized as invisible rather than recognized as essential?
